title: Palkhed Without a Pitched Battle
subtitle: How Bajirao Turned Thirst into a Weapon at Palkhed
region: Pune, Berar, Khandesh, Gujarat, Palkhed and Mungi-Shevgaon
moral: The smartest victory may be won before swords cross.

sources.citation: Selections from the Peshwa Daftar, ed. G.S. Sardesai, letters for the 1727-1728 campaign
sources.note: Administrative correspondence for movements and negotiations.
Documented settlement recognizing Maratha claims after the Palkhed campaign.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, Marathas, Marauders, and State Formation (OUP, 1994)
sources.note: Modern reading of campaigns as revenue and sovereignty operations, not pure conquest.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of a lone rider on a dark horizon, cavalry massed as shadows behind

dialogue.text: Peshwa Bajirao I, in the troubled Deccan of 1727–1728, faces the Nizam’s guns with only speed, thirst, and patience as his chosen weapons.

panels.shot: broad bird’s-eye over the Deccan plateau showing rivers, forts, and marching armies marked by dust plumes

dialogue.text: By the late 1720s the Deccan was a board of rival claims: Mughal farmans, Maratha chauth, old sultanate rights, and the new power of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah.

panels.shot: interior court wide shot of Shaniwar-style wada hall in Pune, low-angle on empty seat of the Peshwa

dialogue.text: In Pune, the young Peshwa Bajirao had already stumbled in early campaigns. Critics whispered that his daring outpaced his caution.

panels.shot: medium close-up across a wooden table map, candlelight on Bajirao’s intense face

dialogue.text: He studied the land instead of his pride: rivers, wells, harvest cycles, the time a bullock cart took to climb a ghat.

panels.shot: interior of the Nizam’s camp tent, low-angle on a richly dressed silhouette against flapping canvas

dialogue.text: To the east, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah gathered a heavy army—artillery, slow baggage, and noble retainers—to check Maratha claims in Berar and Khandesh.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot of cavalry streaming out of Pune gate, tracking shot alongside Bajirao

dialogue.text: In 1727, as the Nizam advanced, Bajirao chose not to guard one fort but to unleash the one thing he had and the Nizam lacked—speed.

panels.shot: wide shot over Berar countryside, low-angle of riders passing burning grain stacks in distance

dialogue.text: He struck Berar, Mahur, Washim—zones rich in revenue. Not for glory alone, but to cut the Nizam’s income and unsettle his rear.

panels.shot: medium shot of Burhanpur’s walls from outside, with distant horsemen on a ridge

dialogue.text: He threatened Burhanpur, Mughal key to the north-south artery, to show that the Maratha spear could reach deep while the Nizam lumbered after him.

panels.shot: close-up on Bajirao in council with a village headman at night by firelight

dialogue.text: Letters from the Peshwa’s daftar show a campaign of persuasion and pressure: village heads warned, supplies diverted, revenue chests moved ahead of the Nizam’s path.

panels.shot: long shot of Nizam’s massive column winding slowly through rough terrain, viewed from a hilltop

dialogue.text: The Nizam followed with dignity but with weight. His artillery and courtly train demanded fodder, grain, and water that Bajirao had already emptied.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bajirao on horseback, gesturing cavalry away from a distant enemy army

dialogue.text: “We do not feed his guns with our dead. We feed his march with hunger.”

panels.shot: close-up of Nizam’s officers in a heated debate inside a field tent

dialogue.text: In the Nizam’s camp, confusion grew. Reports of raided districts, vanished revenue, and empty granaries arrived faster than his troops could march.

panels.shot: wide aerial shot of Palkhed region, highlighting rivers and dry channels under sun

dialogue.text: Bajirao chose his snare near Palkhed, where rivers and streams could be turned into chains if an army depended on them.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bajirao on a ridge overlooking Nizam’s camp near the river, dawn light

dialogue.text: He let the Nizam cross and settle, heavy camp close to the water. Then he closed the circle—fast horse on every approach and ford.

panels.shot: ground-level shot from inside Nizam’s camp, exhausted soldiers eyeing a shrinking waterline

dialogue.text: No grand clash announced their danger. It came slowly, as fodder vanished, grain wagons failed to arrive, and even the river could not serve so many for long.

panels.shot: dramatic wide of Maratha horse arching around the Nizam’s encampment, seen from above and behind Bajirao

dialogue.text: Maratha bands did not storm the camp; they sealed it. Every path that might bring grain or release was shadowed by riders who appeared and vanished with the dust.

panels.shot: close-up of a Nizamite messenger on a tired horse, blocked by calm Maratha riders at a ford

dialogue.text: Messages for help met silent riders at fords and ferries. The great Mughal-trained general found himself trapped not by walls but by emptiness.

panels.shot: interior of the Nizam’s tent, subdued, with the Nizam seated in thought, a letter in hand

dialogue.text: Asaf Jah was no fool; he read the land as well. He knew that each passing day fed Bajirao’s strength and his own army’s weakness.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bajirao receiving emissaries in an open field camp, both sides standing

dialogue.text: So emissaries rode between the camps. The path to peace now ran through Bajirao’s tents, not the Nizam’s cannons.

panels.shot: close-up on hands exchanging a rolled document sealed with cords, neutral background

dialogue.text: On 6 March 1728, at Mungi-Shevgaon, a treaty sealed the Nizam’s acceptance of Maratha claims—an agreement born from empty fields and guarded wells.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bajirao in a quiet moment after the treaty, seated, looking at a map thoughtfully

dialogue.text: For Bajirao, Palkhed was not a legend of invincibility but a lesson: that power lay as much in grain ledgers and water rights as in steel.

panels.shot: wide closing shot of the Deccan landscape at sunset, roads and rivers glowing, faint silhouettes of riders

dialogue.text: The campaign of Palkhed showed India a new kind of war: victory without pitched battle, where the sharpest blade was the mind that reached the river first.
